_about: Hand-written key points for pyt-ophthalmology.html (27 Nov 2026, lead). Samples: FMGE recalls, no images; keys checked.
subject: Ophthalmology
intro: Ophthalmology in FMGE is full of named signs and classic pictures: glaucoma types, cataract surgery, corneal ulcers, the visual pathway and squint. These are the topics that keep coming back, most-asked first, with the one thing to remember about each.

oph.gl.pacg.note: Acute angle closure: sudden painful red eye, halos, headache and vomiting, a fixed mid-dilated oval pupil, very high pressure, shallow anterior chamber; older hypermetropic women. Lower the pressure (IV acetazolamide, pilocarpine once pressure falls), then laser peripheral iridotomy in both eyes.
oph.gl.pacg.why: Sudden painful loss of vision with a mid-dilated pupil is acute angle-closure glaucoma.

oph.gl.poag.note: Open-angle glaucoma: painless, slow, peripheral field loss first; cupping of the optic disc (cup-disc ratio over 0.6, notching). Field defects: arcuate (Bjerrum) scotoma, nasal step. First-line drops: prostaglandin analogues (latanoprost); β-blockers (timolol).

oph.gl.sec.note: Glaucoma in one eye only is usually secondary: after uveitis, trauma (angle recession), lens problems (phacomorphic, phacolytic), steroids, or new vessels (neovascular glaucoma in diabetes and vein occlusion).
oph.gl.sec.why: A raised pressure in only one eye usually has a local cause: secondary glaucoma.

oph.cat.surg.note: Small incision or phaco surgery with an intraocular lens. Trypan blue stains the anterior capsule. After-cataract (posterior capsule opacification): Nd:YAG laser capsulotomy. Endophthalmitis is the dreaded early complication; cystoid macular oedema (Irvine-Gass) comes later.
oph.cat.surg.why: Trypan blue is used to stain and see the anterior lens capsule during surgery.

oph.cat.age.note: Gradual painless blurring of vision, glare, poor night vision. Cortical (cuneiform) and nuclear cataracts are common; posterior subcapsular cataract with steroids and diabetes. Nuclear cataract can cause 'second sight' (better near vision for a while). Treat by surgery when it limits daily life.
oph.cat.age.why: Gradual painless loss of vision with a grey-white lens opacity in an older man is cataract.

oph.cat.cong.note: Named cataracts: Christmas tree (myotonic dystrophy), sunflower (Wilson disease, chalcosis), oil drop (galactosaemia), snowflake (diabetes), rosette (trauma), blue dot (common, harmless). Congenital rubella causes cataract. Remove a dense one early to prevent amblyopia.

oph.uv.ant.note: Pain, redness around the cornea (ciliary flush), photophobia, small irregular pupil, keratic precipitates, cells and flare, hypopyon. Linked to HLA-B27 (ankylosing spondylitis). Treat with steroid drops and a cycloplegic (atropine) to break and prevent posterior synechiae (festooned pupil).
oph.uv.ant.why: Atropine dilates the pupil and breaks the posterior synechiae that cause a festooned pupil.

oph.uv.post.note: Floaters and blurred vision with a quiet eye. Toxoplasma: the commonest cause; a focal necrotising retinochoroiditis next to an old scar with dense vitritis ('headlight in the fog'). CMV retinitis in AIDS (pizza-pie fundus).
oph.uv.post.why: A focal necrotic retinal lesion with heavy vitritis is ocular toxoplasmosis.

oph.uv.assoc.note: HLA-B27 disease: acute anterior uveitis. Behçet: shifting hypopyon, oral and genital ulcers. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis: silent chronic anterior uveitis (screen ANA-positive children). Sarcoidosis: mutton-fat keratic precipitates. Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada: vitiligo, poliosis, meningitis.
oph.uv.assoc.why: In Behçet disease the hypopyon has little fibrin, so it shifts with head position.

oph.cor.viral.note: Herpes simplex: dendritic ulcer with terminal bulbs (fluorescein), reduced corneal sensation. Treat with topical antivirals (aciclovir ointment, ganciclovir gel); never steroids on active epithelial disease. Herpes zoster ophthalmicus: Hutchinson sign (tip of the nose) predicts eye involvement.
oph.cor.viral.why: A dendritic ulcer with terminal bulbs is herpes simplex keratitis, treated with topical aciclovir.

oph.cor.fung.note: Follows injury with vegetable matter (farmers). Dry raised ulcer with feathery edges, satellite lesions, hypopyon that may not move. KOH mount shows hyphae. Treat with natamycin 5% (Fusarium, Aspergillus).

oph.cor.acanth.note: Contact lens wearers, swimming or washing lenses in tap water. Pain far worse than the signs, a ring infiltrate, radial keratoneuritis. Cysts on calcofluor white or in culture on non-nutrient agar with E. coli. Treat with PHMB or chlorhexidine drops.
oph.cor.acanth.why: Contact lenses and contaminated water are risk factors; squamous blepharitis is not.

oph.cor.bact.note: Bacterial ulcers: Pseudomonas (rapid, contact lenses), Staph, Pneumococcus (ulcus serpens with hypopyon). Scrape for Gram stain and culture first, then fortified antibiotic drops (cefazolin with tobramycin) or a fluoroquinolone, every hour.

oph.ret.dr.note: Non-proliferative: microaneurysms (earliest sign), dot-blot haemorrhages, hard exudates, cotton wool spots. Proliferative: new vessels on the disc or elsewhere; treat with pan-retinal photocoagulation (or anti-VEGF). Macular oedema is the commonest cause of vision loss; anti-VEGF injections.
oph.ret.dr.why: New vessels on the disc mean proliferative retinopathy: pan-retinal photocoagulation.

oph.ret.rd.note: Rhegmatogenous detachment (from a retinal break): flashes, floaters, then a curtain over the vision. Risk: high myopia, cataract surgery, trauma. Grey, billowing retina. Treat early with surgery (scleral buckle, vitrectomy, pneumatic retinopexy).
oph.ret.rd.why: A curtain falling over the vision is the classic symptom of retinal detachment.

oph.ret.rp.note: Inherited loss of rods first: night blindness from youth, ring scotoma, tunnel vision. Fundus triad: bony spicule pigment, waxy pale disc, thin arterioles. ERG is reduced early. Linked syndromes: Usher (deafness), Laurence-Moon-Bardet-Biedl.
oph.ret.rp.why: Night blindness getting worse from the teens points to retinitis pigmentosa.

oph.neuro.vp.note: Optic nerve lesion: blindness of that eye. Chiasm (pituitary tumour): bitemporal hemianopia. Optic tract or radiation: homonymous hemianopia on the opposite side. Temporal lobe (Meyer loop): upper quadrant loss ('pie in the sky'). Occipital lesion: homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.
oph.neuro.vp.why: Left homonymous hemianopia means loss of the left half of the field: left temporal and right nasal fields.

oph.neuro.on.note: Young woman, painful eye movements, sudden loss of vision, poor colour vision, relative afferent pupillary defect; the disc often looks normal (retrobulbar). Linked to multiple sclerosis. IV methylprednisolone speeds recovery (Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial).

oph.neuro.pap.note: Swollen discs on both sides from raised intracranial pressure; vision is kept until late (enlarged blind spot). Signs: blurred disc margins, loss of venous pulsation, haemorrhages. Find the cause (tumour, idiopathic intracranial hypertension).

oph.neuro.cn3.note: Third nerve palsy: the eye looks down and out, ptosis, a dilated pupil if the nerve is compressed (posterior communicating aneurysm). Diabetic (ischaemic) palsy usually spares the pupil. Fourth nerve: vertical diplopia worse looking down (stairs), head tilts away. Sixth: eye cannot turn out.
oph.neuro.cn3.why: Down-and-out eye with ptosis is a third nerve palsy.

oph.neuro.horner.note: Horner syndrome: ptosis (mild), miosis, anhidrosis (lack of sweating) on the same side, apparent enophthalmos. Causes: lung apex tumour (Pancoast), carotid dissection, brainstem stroke. Apraclonidine and cocaine drops help confirm it.
oph.neuro.horner.why: Horner syndrome causes loss of sweating (anhidrosis), not excess sweating.

oph.ref.myopia.note: Short-sightedness: light focuses in front of the retina; corrected with concave (minus) lenses. School children squint to see the board. High myopia raises the risk of retinal detachment and glaucoma. Low-dose atropine slows progression in children.
oph.ref.myopia.why: Squinting to see the blackboard (distance) is typical of myopia.

oph.ref.hyper.note: Long-sightedness: light focuses behind the retina; corrected with convex (plus) lenses. Children may get convergent squint (accommodative esotropia). A large difference between the eyes (anisometropia) causes amblyopia in the weaker eye. Hypermetropes are prone to angle-closure glaucoma.
oph.ref.hyper.why: A big difference in power between the eyes (+5D vs +1D) causes anisometropic amblyopia.

oph.ref.astig.note: Unequal curvature of the cornea, so no single focus; corrected with cylindrical lenses. 'With the rule' astigmatism is common in the young. Keratoconus (cone-shaped thinning cornea): irregular astigmatism, Munson sign, Fleischer ring; treat with corneal cross-linking.

oph.sq.para.note: Paralytic squint: double vision worse in the direction of the weak muscle, the deviation varies with gaze, secondary deviation larger than primary. Sixth nerve (the commonest): horizontal diplopia worse looking to the side of the palsy. Fourth nerve: trouble going downstairs, head tilt to the opposite side.
oph.sq.para.why: Vertical double vision worse on looking down, with a head tilt, is a fourth nerve palsy.

oph.sq.tests.note: Hirschberg test: corneal light reflex; each 1 mm shift is about 7° (15 prism dioptres). Cover test finds a manifest squint; alternate cover test finds a latent one (phoria). Treat amblyopia early by patching the good eye.

oph.trauma.chem.note: Alkali burns are worse than acid (they go deeper, saponifying tissue). The first step is immediate, copious irrigation with water or saline for at least 30 minutes, until the pH is normal. Limbal ischaemia predicts the outcome.
oph.trauma.chem.why: Immediate copious irrigation is the single most important step in a chemical burn.

oph.trauma.blunt.note: Hyphaema (blood in the anterior chamber), angle recession (later glaucoma), Vossius ring on the lens, commotio retinae (Berlin oedema), blow-out fracture of the orbital floor (diplopia on looking up, numb cheek, teardrop sign).
oph.trauma.blunt.why: Blood collected in the anterior chamber after blunt injury is a hyphaema.

oph.trauma.pen.note: Signs: a peaked pupil, shallow chamber, prolapsed uveal tissue, low pressure. Shield the eye, no pressure, no drops; X-ray or CT for a foreign body (no MRI if metal). Siderosis from retained iron, chalcosis from copper.

oph.trauma.so.note: Sympathetic ophthalmia: a bilateral granulomatous uveitis weeks to months after a penetrating injury to one eye (uveal antigens exposed). Dalen-Fuchs nodules. Prevented by removing a badly injured eye within about 2 weeks; treated with steroids.

oph.conj.trach.note: Chlamydia trachomatis A-C, the leading infectious cause of blindness. Follicles, Herbert pits, Arlt line (scar on the upper tarsal conjunctiva), trichiasis, corneal scarring. WHO SAFE strategy: Surgery, Antibiotics (azithromycin), Facial cleanliness, Environmental improvement.
oph.conj.trach.why: S in SAFE stands for surgery, to correct trichiasis.

oph.conj.allerg.note: Vernal keratoconjunctivitis: boys, warm weather, intense itching, ropy discharge, cobblestone papillae on the upper lid, Horner-Trantas dots, shield ulcer. Treat with mast cell stabilisers and antihistamines; short steroid courses for flares.

oph.conj.tum.note: Pterygium: a triangular fold growing onto the cornea from the nasal side, linked to sunlight; remove with a conjunctival autograft to stop recurrence. Pinguecula does not reach the cornea. Ocular surface squamous neoplasia is linked to HIV and HPV.

oph.lid.ptosis.note: Congenital ptosis: weak levator. Marcus Gunn jaw-winking: the eyelid lifts on chewing (misdirected fifth nerve). Acquired: aponeurotic (old age), myasthenia (fatigable), third nerve palsy, Horner (mild). Surgery depends on levator function.
oph.lid.ptosis.why: A ptotic lid that lifts with jaw movement is Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome.

oph.lac.nld.note: Congenital nasolacrimal duct block (valve of Hasner): watering and discharge in infants. Massage (Crigler) until about 1 year; probing if it persists. Adults: dacryocystitis; dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR) for chronic blockage.

oph.tum.rb.note: Retinoblastoma: the commonest eye cancer in children; RB1 gene on chromosome 13 (two-hit). Leucocoria (white pupil, cat's eye reflex) is the commonest sign, then squint. Calcification on CT; Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes. Survivors of the inherited type risk osteosarcoma.
oph.tum.rb.why: Retinoblastoma is caused by mutations in the RB gene.

oph.comm.vita.note: WHO xerophthalmia stages: XN night blindness (earliest), X1A conjunctival xerosis, X1B Bitot spots, X2 corneal xerosis, X3A/X3B corneal ulcer and keratomalacia, XS scars, XF fundus changes. Treat with vitamin A on day 1, day 2 and after 2 weeks.
oph.comm.vita.why: Bitot's spots are stage X1B in the WHO classification.

oph.inst.title: Eye investigations and instruments
oph.inst.note: Applanation tonometry (Goldmann) is the gold standard for eye pressure. Gonioscopy views the angle. A-scan biometry measures eye length for the lens power. Potential acuity meter predicts vision after cataract surgery. OCT images the macula and nerve fibre layer.
oph.inst.why: A potential acuity meter estimates how well the eye will see after the cataract is removed.
